00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:11.720: A sustained, resonant bell tone, clear and pure, rings out with a long decay, filling the space with a gentle, vibrating hum. No speech, no other sounds.

00:00:11.720 --> 00:00:13.000: The bell tone fades out completely. Silence.

00:00:13.000 --> 00:00:14.000: A male voice begins speaking, calm and measured: “What is Nirvana?”

00:00:14.000 --> 00:00:29.000: The same male voice continues: “Nirvana is when everything the mind makes comes to a stop. The letting go of everything carried, the thirst ends, nothing pulls you anymore, stopping.”

00:00:29.000 --> 00:00:37.000: The male voice continues: “Going out like a flame with no fuel.”

00:00:37.000 --> 00:00:48.000: The male voice continues: “This is peaceful, this is excellent, namely the stilling of all preparations, the relinquishment of all assets, the destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction.”

00:00:48.000 --> 00:00:50.000: Silence.

00:00:50.000 --> 00:00:52.000: A different male voice, slightly higher in pitch and with a questioning tone, asks: “Why don’t I see Nirvana right now?”

00:00:52.000 --> 00:01:04.000: The first male voice responds: “You do not see Nirvana right now because you imagine a seer and a world, and neither is there.”

00:01:04.000 --> 00:01:15.000: The first male voice continues: “What is called ‘manana’ is the imagining in egoistic terms, imparting reality to illusory things.”

00:01:15.000 --> 00:01:25.000: The first male voice continues: “Only a looking is there, nothing worth looking at. Only a seeing is there, nothing to be seen.”

00:01:25.000 --> 00:01:35.000: The first male voice continues: “The law of dependent arising is already implicated. There is therefore no seer apart from the phenomenon of seeing, according to the Tathagata.”

00:01:35.000 --> 00:01:37.000: Silence.

00:01:37.000 --> 00:01:39.000: The second male voice asks: “What keeps it going?”

00:01:39.000 --> 00:01:50.000: The first male voice responds: “First keeps it going, impelled by that making it into something, it runs towards the mirage, the gap is ignored. What impels one to ignore that gap is thirst.”

00:01:50.000 --> 00:01:54.00

The text reads:

“...the term papancha is that it conveys the sense of proliferation and complexity of thought, on the lines of those three basic tendencies. That is why the person concerned is said to be overwhelmed by papancha-sañña-saṅkhāra. Here we need to clarify for ourselves the meaning of the word saṅkhāra. According to the commentary, it means papancha-sañña-saṅkhāra-ti etta-saṅkhāra-ti kottāsu. From this we can infer the fact that the happiness unaccompanied by thinking and pondering is nearer to nibbāna. This is the criterion we can glean from this discussion. In the same way, the Buddha goes on to analyze unhappiness as being twofold. Out of them, that which is productive of unskillful thoughts should be avoided, and that which is productive of skillful thoughts should be pursued. But therein too, that which is unaccompanied by thinking and pondering is declared as more excellent than that which is accompanied by thinking and pondering. That is the path to nibbāna. So also is the case with regard to the analysis of equanimity. Therein, that equanimity productive of skillful thoughts has to be pursued, subject to the proviso that equanimity unaccompanied by thinking and pondering is more excellent than that which is so accompanied. In summing up, the Buddha concludes the explanation with the sentence: ‘Evaṃ patipanno kho, devānaṃ inda, bhikkhu papancha-sañña-saṅkhāra-nirodha-sārūpaṃ bhāgāmini patipadāṃ patipanno hoti.’ It is a monk who has thus set out talking of gods, who is treading the path of practice conducive to the cessation of reckonings born of prolific perceptions. He does not delight in nibbāna. Why so? Because he knows that delighting is the root of suffering, and from becoming comes birth, and to the one become there is decay and death. It seems then that the Tathāgata does not delight in nibbāna, because delighting is the root of suffering. Now, nandi is a form of grasping upādāna, impaired by craving. It is sometimes expressly called an upādāna: ‘ya vedeṇāsu nandi taddupādānaṃ.’ Whatever delighting there is in feeling, that is a grasping. When there is delighting, there is a grasping. When there is grasping, there is bhava, becoming or existence. From becoming comes birth, and to the one who has thus come to be, there is decay and death. Because of contact, feeling — what one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one reasons about. What one reasons about, one turns into papancha. 00:00:05.000 --> 00:00:06.000: The male voice continues: “Then it will not carry you, nothing to stand on, nowhere to land, neither here, nor there, nor in between.”

00:00:09.000 --> 00:00:10.000: The male voice continues: “And when ‘by’ you are not in it, then ‘by’ you are neither here, nor there, nor in between.”

00:00:10.000 --> 00:00:11.000: The male voice continues: “This itself is the end of suffering.”
